title: Malbim on Nehemiah
text: In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes—the same Artaxerxes discussed in the Book of Ezra. This makes it clear that this book is a continuation of the preceding Book of Ezra. As our Sages said in Sanhedrin (93b), “After all, Nehemiah related all the matters recorded by Ezra.” Likewise, in the enumeration of the twenty-four books of Scripture, these two books are counted as one book; otherwise, the verse would have needed to specify which year of Artaxerxes’ reign it meant.

The questions:
(2) The expression “the remnant who were left there” implies that he did not inquire about those who had returned from captivity in the days of Cyrus?

And I asked them: first, about the Jews, and second, about Jerusalem. They answered the first question first and the second question afterward, as Rashi explains. However, from the precise wording “the remnant who were left,” it appears that the Jews who returned with the permission of Cyrus, and later with the permission of Artaxerxes, had their own governor (Ezra 5:14). He therefore asked specifically about the Jews who had already been living there, who were under the authority of the governors of the province Beyond the River (as appears below, 3:7). They were suffering misery and humiliation because the governors oppressed them. It is concerning them that the verse says, “who were left.” By contrast, the Jews who had returned there from captivity had their own governor to protect and shelter them.
The great God: Daniel likewise began his prayer with these words (Daniel 9:4); see my commentary there.

Attentive: This is an adjective formed on the same pattern as oreri (“those who awaken me”), as Ibn Ezra and Radak explain. And may Your eyes be open—so that You will immediately attend to fulfilling the request through Your Providence. Daniel likewise said this (Daniel 9:18). Today, day and night: The prayer that I am offering today is one that I pray continually, day and night, as stated, “I mourned for days,” and “I was fasting and praying.” And I means: and I confess that I and my father’s household have sinned.

The questions:
(7) The commentators struggled to explain the expression “We have acted very corruptly” (ḥavol ḥavalnu)?

“We have given You a pledge” (ḥavol ḥavalnu lakh): The expression relates to collateral or a pledge, and ḥavol is a noun rather than an infinitive, as the commentators explain. It portrays Israel as obligated to observe God’s Torah. When they fail to pay this debt, God takes everything precious to them—the Temple and the Holy Land—as collateral for their sins, until they fulfill their obligation; He will then return the Temple to them. Thus it is written, “Why should God become angry at your voice and seize the work of your hands?” Similarly, our Sages said: “Why was it called the Mishkan? Because it was taken as a pledge on account of Israel’s sins.” The meaning is: We have given You pledges, but we have not observed the commandments and have not paid the debt. The metaphor depicts Israel as having given the pledge; for this reason, the phrase is connected with the preposition lamed—“to You”—because they brought this upon themselves through their sins.

Remember: Did You not command Moses, saying, “If you act unfaithfully”? The term me’ilah, “acting unfaithfully,” is used of someone who betrays another by denying possession of a deposit or something entrusted to his hand, or of someone who misappropriates consecrated property. That is, you will act unfaithfully regarding His commandments, which you obligated yourselves to observe. “I will scatter you among the nations” and take your land as collateral. “But if you return”—if you repent and pay the debt, I will return the collateral to you. “I will bring them to the place”—he uses the phrase “which You commanded Moses” because repentance is a positive commandment.

And they are Your servants: Although they returned to the Land of Israel with the permission of the Persian kings, You brought them out of Egypt with great power, signs, and wonders. It is therefore fitting that now, too—as in the days when we departed from the land of Egypt—You should show us wonders.

Behold, O Hashem: Do not say that at that time they were deserving because of the righteous people who lived in that generation. Even now, let Your ear be attentive to the prayer of Your servant and to the prayer of Your servants, for they too desire to fear Your name. It is therefore fitting that You act in the merit of their prayers and deeds. And grant me success: In their merit, cause me to succeed, so that the king will grant my request. And I: Because he had referred merely to “this man” without identifying him, he explains that I was the king’s cupbearer. It was concerning the king that I prayed to find compassion in his sight.

The questions:
(1) Is the verb governing the word “wine” missing from the verse? And what is the meaning of “I had never been sad in his presence”? Is this not contradicted by the fact that his countenance was sad?

And it came to pass—wine was before him: The statement “I was the king’s cupbearer” applies to both clauses: “And I was serving wine before him.” In the second clause, serving refers to the actual act of pouring the wine. And I had not been sad: The king insisted that his servants not appear before him with a gloomy countenance, because he would then suspect them of harboring evil intentions. Nehemiah knew the king’s temperament and took care to appear cheerful whenever he came before him. He therefore says that, in truth, I had never been sad in his presence.

And he said: Nevertheless, the king noticed that Nehemiah’s countenance was sad and became angry about it. This may have been because the signs of his fasting and self-affliction during those days were visible on his face; alternatively, it occurred through Divine Providence, so that the king would question him and thereby give him an opportunity to speak. Nehemiah became afraid, because “a king’s wrath is like messengers of death,” for he knew that the king regarded such behavior as an offense.

And I said: He therefore did not deny that his countenance was sad. Instead, he explained that the reason was that the city containing the graves of his ancestors lay in ruins, for the burial place of one’s ancestors was precious and sacred in the eyes of the Persians.

The questions:
(4) When he says, “And I prayed,” how could he have prayed while standing before the king, and why does he not record the text of the prayer?

For what: That is, what exactly do you request—that the graves be rebuilt, or the entire city? Do you want me to order it rebuilt, or do you wish to be the one who rebuilds it? And I prayed: While answering the king, he inwardly addressed God in prayer. When he said, “If it pleases the king,” in his heart he directed these words toward the supreme King, praying that the matter should be pleasing in His sight and that He should favor the work of his hands; but aloud, he addressed these words to the earthly king.

If: That is, if the matter itself—rebuilding the ruined city—is good in his sight, and if your servant finds favor to serve as the agent for this purpose. Thus he said, “If your servant finds favor, send me; and if it pleases the king, I will rebuild it.”

The questions:
(6) Should the verse not have said, “And I gave him a time, and he sent me”?

And he said: The meaning is that both the king and the consort sitting beside him spoke to Nehemiah, just as in the verse, “And Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said.” According to the Sages, this king was Darius, the son of Esther. Accordingly, it may be suggested that this consort was his mother Esther, who hastened to make this request—for the king had already consented to the matter—because of her love for her people and her birthplace. How long: That is, when will you depart, and when will you return? And it pleased: Even before Nehemiah had settled upon a definite period, the matter pleased the king, and he sent me—that is, he granted me permission to go. Only afterward, I gave him a time, answering the king’s question concerning the time of his departure and return.

The questions:
(7) What is the meaning of “that they may let me pass”? And who was to escort him until he reached the governors?

Let letters be given to me: The king’s scribes should issue them in the king’s name, so that they may escort me with troops and horsemen for protection; for the king provided him with army officers as far as the province Beyond the River (verse 9).

The keeper of the royal forest: He was responsible for the forests of Lebanon that belonged to the king. To make beams: The word is an infinitive in the intensive conjugation, meaning to make roofing for the gates of the fortress—that is, the gates of the Temple Mount. At that time, only the Temple itself had been built, but not the surrounding complex. And for the house into which I shall enter: The king would build a residence in every province for its governor, and that house belonged to the king. He therefore did not say, “for my house.”

And the king sent: This explains who escorted him as far as the governors. Until that point, he was accompanied by the army officers whom the king had sent with him. From his request that letters be given to the governors so that they would conduct him onward from there, it is evident that he had requested the king’s troops to protect him until he reached them.

The questions:
(12–18) Why did he not tell anyone what he intended to do? Why did he inspect the wall at night? Why did he leave through the Valley Gate and return through the same gate? Why did he not tell the officials where he had gone? All these matters are obscure riddles, especially since he told them immediately afterward what he intended to do, as stated in verse 18.

And I arose at night: He did not yet wish to reveal that he intended to rebuild the wall, lest the enemies immediately begin to obstruct and denounce the undertaking, as they attempted to do afterward. He therefore went at night with only a few men, and they traveled on foot so that their passage would cause no commotion.

And I went out through the Valley Gate: Nehemiah’s residence was located there. This is clearly demonstrated by the account below (chapter 12): one of the two thanksgiving processions went to the right, toward the Dung Gate (12:31), while the second went to the left, toward the Tower of the Ovens (12:38). Evidently, both processions departed from the Valley Gate, which stood between the Tower of the Ovens and the Dung Gate (3:11–14). They departed from there because the governor’s residence was located there. The Valley Gate was on the western side. Nehemiah left his residence heading south, passed the place called the Dragon’s Spring, and proceeded to the Dung Gate, which was one thousand cubits away (3:13). And I was breaking: It appears that he wanted to test whether the portions of the old wall that remained were strong enough that they would not need to be demolished, so that only the breached sections would have to be filled in. Thus it is stated below (4:1), “the breaches began to be closed,” implying that wherever the wall was not breached, they left the old wall standing. He therefore tested whether he could break a standing section with his hand or whether it was strong. Ibn Ezra’s version spells the word with a sin rather than a shin, and he interprets it as related to thought or consideration—meaning that Nehemiah examined the wall. This interpretation fits very well with what I have explained.

And I passed by the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool: This was along his route southward (below, 3:15). And there was no room: He could not ride there because the breaches were narrow, so he dismounted and proceeded on foot.

And I went up through the valley: He continued southward throughout, and says, “I went up,” as it is written there, “as far as the stairs that descend from the City of David.” And I returned: From there he began retracing the route he had taken, traveling from south to north until he reached the Valley Gate, where he had begun his journey; from there he returned to his residence.

And the officials: They noticed that he was not at his residence, but they did not know where he had gone or what he was doing, because he had not told them at all for what purpose he had come to Jerusalem. Thus he says, “to the Jews,” and so forth, “until then”—that is, until that day I had not told anyone about the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Only now did he begin to speak to them about it.

And I said to them, “You see the distress”: That is, the reason we suffer at the hands of Judah’s enemies is that Jerusalem lies in ruins, and there is no fortified stronghold in which to take refuge from the enemy. Therefore, come, let us rebuild, so that we will no longer be an object of disgrace, for then we will have a fortified stronghold.

The king: A decree had already been issued by Cyrus to halt this construction (Ezra 4:21), and “a document written in the king’s name cannot be revoked.” However, that decree stated only that the city was not to be rebuilt “until a command is issued by me.” The king could therefore issue a new order granting permission, and they now possessed such authorization. This is what Nehemiah told them.

And I answered them: He first answered that the undertaking had the king’s authorization. And I said to them: Afterward, he told them, “The God of heaven”—that is, we have a share in Jerusalem, for it is our ancestral inheritance, as well as a memorial, because the God of heaven will grant us success, and the work of our hands will remain as a memorial and an act of righteousness. For we are His servants and are building for the sake of God; therefore, we shall arise and build. But you have no share, because you are foreigners; nor any right, because you do not serve God; nor any memorial through your deeds, because God will not grant you success.

And they built the Sheep Gate: The Sheep Gate was situated at the center of the eastern wall. From there, they built northward, then from north to west, and from the west they turned eastward along the southern side, until they once again reached the Sheep Gate. The Tower of Hananel was north of the Sheep Gate; farther north stood the Tower of the Hundred, followed by the Fish Gate. The account begins with the Sheep Gate, at the center of the eastern wall, because it stood directly opposite the Temple. This is evident from chapter 12, where the two thanksgiving processions that departed from the Valley Gate, at the center of the western wall, met one another there and proceeded from there to the Temple. Thus it says, “They consecrated it,” because it stood opposite the Temple.
And next to him they built: They built the section between the Tower of Hananel and the Fish Gate.

And the Fish Gate: It appears that wherever the term “built” is used, the wall had already collapsed and had to be rebuilt entirely. Wherever the term “repaired” is used, however, it was necessary only to reinforce the old wall and seal its breaches.

But their nobles: This may be explained in light of verse 7, which says that the people of Gibeon and Mizpah were under the authority of the governor of the province Beyond the River because they had lived in Judah from earlier times, as explained there. Accordingly, the Tekoites likewise had not returned in the days of Cyrus but had already been living there, and were therefore under the authority of that governor. Nevertheless, their nobles did not submit their necks to the work of their masters, because they were powerful men and enjoyed independence. Alternatively, the Tekoites had a leader who ruled over them, and he and his men built this section; but among them was a group of nobles who refused to obey the command of their lord, the leader. They therefore separated from the others and built independently, as stated in verse 27: “After him, the Tekoites repaired a second section.”
And the Old Gate: It was situated at the northeastern corner. In my opinion, this gate was also called the Corner Gate, where Uzziah built towers (II Chronicles 26), as we shall explain in verse 8.

Under the seat of the governor of the province Beyond the River: This accords with what was explained in verse 5. Those who had returned with Zerubbabel or Ezra had Zerubbabel—and afterward Nehemiah—as their governor. Those who had already been living in Judah, however, remained subject to the former governor of the province Beyond the River, who already exercised authority over them. The people of Jericho (verse 2) and the sons of Hassenaah (verse 3) had returned in the days of Ezra, but the people of Gibeon and Mizpah were not listed among those who returned (Ezra 2). They therefore belonged under the jurisdiction and authority of the governor of the province Beyond the River and acted with his permission. The same applies to the Tekoites, as explained in verse 5.

And they fortified Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall: From what is stated below (12:38–39), the Ephraim Gate—which is not mentioned here—stood between the Broad Wall and the Old Gate. This is the section that Joash breached, extending four hundred cubits from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate (II Chronicles 25). The Corner Gate was the Old Gate, situated at the northeastern corner. We must therefore say that the Ephraim Gate had not been so severely destroyed; consequently, its rebuilding is not mentioned separately but is included with the wall as a whole. The expression “and they fortified” means that they strengthened and reinforced it. On the northern side, Jerusalem was not surrounded by mountains but by level ground, so they had to strengthen that area more extensively, as far as the Broad Wall, where the wall served as protection against the enemy.
And opposite his house: He also repaired the entire section of the wall facing his house, in addition to the section beside Rephaiah that he repaired beyond his house, toward the east.

A second section: Because there were no gates or towers on that side, they divided the length of the wall into two sections. They repaired the second section as far as the Tower of the Ovens, which stood at the western corner.

And next to him: From this point, the text enumerates the western side from north to south. Shallum repaired the section from the Tower of the Ovens to the Valley Gate. Hallohesh: The letter heh is part of the name’s root, as I have explained several times.

The Valley Gate … they built it: Merely repairing and strengthening it was insufficient, as explained above; it had to be rebuilt. From there, they repaired a section extending one thousand cubits to the Dung Gate.

And the Dung Gate and the Fountain Gate: The wall extending from the Valley Gate continued to the Dung Gate, and from there to the Fountain Gate. Close to it, toward the east and within the wall, were the waters of Shiloah, also called the King’s Pool (above, 2:14), where the king’s gardens were located. It is known that the Fortress of Zion, the City of David, Solomon’s palace, the Millo, and the House of Millo stood on the eastern slope of Mount Zion. From there, steps descended by way of the Valley of Ben-Hinnom and the city wall toward the king’s gardens and the pool. The City of David was west of the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, within the wall of Mount Zion, while the garden and the pool were within the city wall. A bridge was built across the two walls, enabling passage from one to the other. This is the meaning of “and the wall of the Pool of Shiloah by the King’s Garden, as far as the stairs descending” from the City of David.

After him: This wall, which was doubled—and was therefore called “the two walls”—continued southward opposite the tombs of the House of David, which were on the heights of Mount Zion. There in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom was also a reservoir later constructed to collect the water, as stated: “You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the Old Pool.” Thus the verse says, “as far as opposite the tombs of David, and as far as the constructed pool”—that is, the pool constructed afterward—“and as far as the House of the Mighty Men,” where the warriors would assemble. South of it, at the southwestern corner, was the armory. This is the meaning of verse 19: “opposite the ascent to the armory at the corner,” meaning that the weapons were brought up there. I have already explained above the expression “a second section.” It may also mean that wherever the text says “a second section,” the builder undertook two measured portions: they measured and estimated how much each person would accept responsibility for, and that builder accepted two such portions. All the other occurrences may be interpreted in the same way.

Harhaiah: This is the name of a person. The word “repaired” in the preceding verse and the word “after him” each apply to two clauses: “After him, Harhaiah [repaired]”; “[after him], Baruch repaired.” From the corner: The account now begins to describe the southern side, proceeding from west to east.
Meremoth: He was already mentioned in verse 4. The text therefore says “a second section,” because he built two sections.

Binnui son of Henadad—a second section: He had repaired the first section together with his kinsmen, as stated in verses 17–18: “Rehum son of Bani” and “Hashabiah, their kinsman,” who were descendants of Henadad. As far as the corner and as far as the turret: This was the southeastern corner. There was also a pinnah there, a type of tower, as in “against the fortified cities and against the high turrets” (Zephaniah 1), and “to be upon the towers and upon the turrets” (II Chronicles 26:15).

Opposite the corner: The king’s palace stood opposite it, toward the east, and from there extended the tower projecting from the king’s palace, which belonged to the court of the guard, itself located beside the king’s palace. This is not the Guard Gate mentioned below (12:39), which was near the Temple. The word “repaired” in the preceding verse applies to four clauses: “Palal son of Uzai [repaired]”; “after him, Pedaiah son of Parosh [repaired].” And the Temple servants—who lived on the Ophel—repaired as far as opposite the Water Gate. The Temple servants repaired the tower projecting from the king’s palace and, from there, the section as far as the Water Gate, which stood on the eastern side; for the text now enumerates the eastern wall from south to north. Yoma 69a indicates that the Water Gate stood opposite the Temple.

The Tekoites—a second section: As explained above in verse 5. As far as the wall of the Ophel: The Ophel was a separate fortress, situated at some distance from the great tower projecting from the king’s palace. It appears that they built there along the wall, between the tower and the Ophel connected opposite it. The Temple servants built the city wall as far as the Water Gate, together with the projecting tower itself. The Tekoites built the wall from opposite the tower as far as the wall of the Ophel. The Horse Gate was located there and likewise stood opposite the king’s palace, as mentioned in II Kings 11:16, for a road led from the Horse Gate to the king’s palace.
The keeper of the East Gate of the Temple courtyard; this was the Inspection Gate mentioned in verse 31.

The sixth: He was Zalaph’s sixth son. A second: The masculine form sheni has the same meaning as the feminine shenit, “a second section.” His chamber: That is, his room, for it stood opposite the Temple courtyard. Likewise, the Inspection Gate was the eastern gate of the Temple, as stated in tractate Middot.

And as far as the upper chamber at the corner: There was a fortified position there to which people ascended, because it stood on elevated ground. After it came the Sheep Gate, from which they had begun rebuilding.

And it displeased him: The expression ḥarah lo means that something was evil in his eyes, as in “and Cain was greatly displeased.” Thus the Sages explained, “David was displeased”—his face changed and became like a scorched cake. Anger arises when this displeasure is outwardly expressed, and afterward comes mockery.

Will they fortify it for themselves? The expression denotes strengthening, as in “and they fortified Jerusalem” (above, verse 8). Will they strengthen the wall? Will they offer sacrifices and finish it in a day? Will they offer sacrifices so that, through the merit of those sacrifices, a miracle will be performed for them and the work completed in a single day? Or will a miracle be performed for them to revive the stones that had already “died” and lay buried in heaps of dust, though they were burned? Figuratively, he applied the concepts of death and life to the stones.

And Tobiah: He added that even if they succeeded in completing the construction, it would not constitute a fortified structure, for even a fox could breach it. Foxes commonly make openings among ruins, as it is written, “Your prophets, O Israel, were like foxes among ruins” (Ezekiel 13:4).

Hear: First, repay them for the contempt with which they scorned us. Second, do not cover their iniquity in provoking the builders, for they sought actively to hinder them from their work. Concerning the words “and let not their sin be blotted out,” see Jeremiah 18:23.

So we built: Nevertheless, not only was the work not halted because of them, but the people had a heart to work; their enemies’ actions did not cause any laziness or discouragement to enter their hearts.

For the wall was being healed: The term arukhah properly denotes the joining together of a bone that has been broken in two (Jeremiah 30:17); it is used here figuratively for the breaches in the wall. The breaches: The breached places in the wall had begun to be closed.

And to cause confusion within it: It is evident that they were afraid to engage in open warfare. Instead, they sought to mislead the inhabitants of Jerusalem and attack them suddenly, when they would not be on their guard against them, as stated in verse 5.
Against them: That is, to keep watch on them and give warning when they attacked the city.

The questions:
(4–6) These verses are exceedingly difficult to understand.

And Judah said: The people of Judah said that construction of the wall now had to be suspended for two reasons. First, the strength of the burden-bearers had failed. The word refers to a person who carries burdens, as in “seventy thousand burden-bearers” (II Chronicles 2). And there was much rubble; as long as the burden-bearers had not cleared away the rubble, we would be unable to build the wall.

Second, they said: Our enemies are lying in wait to attack us suddenly. They said to one another, “We will come upon them unexpectedly, so that they will not know of it beforehand, for we will keep our plan secret. Nor will they see us as we approach, until we come into their midst, because we will attack them from a place of concealment.”

And it came to pass: This too is part of the report of the people of Judah, explaining how they learned of the plot. When the Jews who lived near them came to Jerusalem—that is, the Jews who lived in the cities of Judah’s enemies—they told us ten times. They did not tell us this only once, in which case it might have been dismissed as a fabrication, but repeated it many times. Nor did the reports come from only one place, in which case one might have thought that only some of the enemies intended us harm; rather, they came from all the places, showing that all of Judah’s hostile neighbors had agreed upon the plan. “You must return to us” is what the people of Judah said to one another. They meant: You cannot disperse, each man apart from his fellow, to build the wall. Instead, all of you must cease and rest from building and join us, so that we may stand together in one place, arrayed for battle against the enemy, now that we know with certainty that he will attack us. Moreover, the Jews who came there had revealed the specific place from which the enemy would attack; they therefore had to take their stand at that location, prepared for battle.

The questions:
(7–8) Why does he say “and I stationed” twice? What is the meaning of “and I saw”—what did he see?

And I stationed: Once Nehemiah had learned precisely from the Jewish informants the place from which the enemies would attack, he stationed men in the lower parts of that location, where the enemies were expected to arrive. Behind the wall, he stationed warriors in a concealed ambush. They hid behind the wall in the barren, rocky places—tzeḥiḥim, as in “a barren rock”—beneath the rocks, so that when the enemies arrived, they could fire upon them from ambush. And I stationed the people by their families: At that same location, he also stationed the people openly against the enemy, divided by families into separate companies. All of them—both those lying in ambush behind the wall and those standing openly for battle—had their swords and spears and were prepared to fight.

And I saw: Nehemiah, standing as a watchman, saw that the enemy was coming and approaching that place. And I arose and said: He then warned the people that the sword was approaching and told them not to be afraid, but to remember Hashem and fight.

And it came to pass: As a result, our enemies heard that their plan had become known to us, for they found all of us arrayed for battle. God thereby frustrated their scheme, and they withdrew without beginning to fight at all. Then, when we saw that the danger had passed, we all returned to the wall.

The questions:
(10–15) In verse 11, he says that even those engaged in the work held weapons, whereas verse 15 says that half were engaged in the work and half held the spears. In verse 11, he says that the builders held a weapon in one hand, whereas verse 12 says that the builders’ swords were strapped to their waists. How are these statements to be reconciled?

And it came to pass from that day onward: It appears that at first they still feared that the enemy might return against them. They therefore did not yet disperse, each man to his own place—for each family had been building a different section around the wall—but all remained at this particular place, where the danger was greatest, since the enemy had seen that this location was favorable for attacking them. They all built together in one place. At that time, the people were not divided so that half performed the work while half held weapons. Rather, everyone held a weapon in one hand and worked with the other, as stated in verses 11–12. Only Nehemiah’s young men and servants, who were mighty warriors, were divided: half of my young men performed the work, and half held—that is, held weapons. The verse then explains why Nehemiah’s young men alone were assigned this task, with half of them performing no work: they possessed spears, shields, bows, and armor. Those who fought with spears also carried shields, while those who fought with bows wore armor. They could not perform the work, because the spearmen held a spear in one hand and a shield in the other, while the archers wore armor, and it was impossible to work while wearing scale armor. They were trained warriors, experienced in fighting with shields and armor in the manner of soldiers. And the officers were behind all the house of Judah: The officers and the entire house of Judah were all there behind me—that is, they remained assembled around Nehemiah and did not disperse to their respective tasks. Since they were not trained warriors and possessed neither shields and armor nor bows—for archery requires training—they followed a different arrangement: all of them worked with one hand while holding a weapon in the other, so that they could stab any enemy who approached them. This is what the following verse explains.

Those who built: Both those who built the wall and those who carried burdens were alike in this respect. The verse explains that those carrying burdens had the loads placed upon them. There is a distinction between massa, “a burden,” and ma’amasa, “a load placed upon someone”: the latter is a burden that another person places upon the carrier, whereas “carrying” can also refer to a person lifting the burden himself, as I explained in Isaiah 46. Thus, they did not place the burdens upon their own shoulders; rather, each person placed the load upon his fellow’s shoulder, which is called omes. The verse explains why: with one hand he performed the work, while the other held the weapon. Since it is impossible to lift a burden onto one’s shoulder with only one hand, each person had to load it onto his fellow’s shoulder.

And the builders: Since it was impossible to build with one hand while holding a weapon in the other, each man built with his sword fastened at his waist. A builder could easily draw his sword when the enemy approached, unlike a burden-bearer, whose load would prevent him from doing so; the burden-bearers therefore held their weapons in their hands. There is a distinction between a shelaḥ and a sword: the shelaḥ is a blade sharpened on both edges and used for thrusting. It is not kept in a sheath but held in the hand like a spear. And the one who sounded the shofar was beside me, ready to give battle signals whenever necessary.

And I said: This was the situation at first. Later, however, when they saw that the enemy had returned to his own place and was not coming back against them, their great fear subsided. Each man then began returning to the place where he was building—the section of the wall that he had undertaken to build. Nehemiah therefore told them that, since the work was extensive and spread out, each person had to work in a different place, for if they all remained in one location, the work would never be completed. Consequently, we are separated along the wall, each man at his own workplace, and from now on we will be far from one another. I therefore command you, first, that wherever you hear the sound of the shofar, you must assemble there with us. And secondly, from now on—

And we: Not everyone would engage in the work, but only half of them. And half would hold the spears, patrolling throughout the city to guard it. Since the people were now scattered and separated, there would be no benefit in having those engaged in the work carry their weapons, for in any event a few individuals at a single location could not fight effectively. Instead, they would perform their work normally, while the other half would stand together closely on guard with spears, ready to confront the enemy.
And they served us: At night they served as a guard, and by day they performed the work.

We did not: The word ein (“not”) is repeated implicitly in the following clause: “We did not take off [our clothes at night]; [nor did] any man send his garment to the water”—that is, no one sent his garment to a launderer to be washed in water.

And there was: The outcry of the poor among the people against the wealthy was great. The verse explains that those who cried out comprised two groups. The first group complained about the future, because they had no means of sustaining themselves; their complaints were divided into two kinds.

Some said, “We are pledging our sons and daughters at interest”: That is, we will be compelled to pledge our sons and daughters as security and borrow money against them at interest, so that we may obtain grain and live. These were people who owned no fields and had no means of sustaining themselves. [The word rabbim is a verb derived from the term for interest or increase, as in “Woe to him who increases what is not his” (Habakkuk 2:6), and, according to my interpretation, “You did not gain an increase from their price” (Psalms 44:13).]

And there were others who owned fields and vineyards. They said, “We are pledging our fields”—that is, we have been compelled to provide our fields as security, namely, as collateral—so that we may obtain grain during the famine. Although a field’s produce ordinarily provides bread for the one who sows it, now it was a time of famine and the land had not yielded its produce. They were therefore compelled to pledge their fields in order to obtain food. [Here the verse does not say, “We are borrowing at interest,” because they would not have to pay interest: the lender would consume the field’s produce and thereby receive compensation for allowing them continued use of the money.]

And there were others: The second group complained about what had already occurred. They said, “We borrowed money” during the previous year, even though it was not a year of famine, because we were required to pay the king’s tax—the word middah denotes taxation, as in “tribute, tax, and toll”—and we pledged our fields and vineyards during that year. [The verb “we are pledging” from the preceding verse applies here as well.]

And now, when money is needed to buy bread because it is a year of famine, surely our flesh is like the flesh of our brothers, and we too deserve to eat bread; our children are like their children, and it is fitting that ours should likewise not become slaves. Yet we are subjecting our sons—that is, we will be compelled to sell them as slaves in exchange for bread—and some of our daughters have already been subjected as maidservants. The word “subjected” also implies that they are treated as though they were without protection and may be abused, as in, “Will he even assault the queen?” And it is not within our power to redeem them, because our fields and vineyards have belonged to others since the previous year.

And I became angry: First, he was angered by the outcry of the poor in the first group, who complained that charity was being withheld from them; and second, by these matters—the outcry of the second group, who complained of oppression and injustice.

And my heart took counsel within me: My heart clothed itself with a spirit of kingship and authority, so that I would show no favoritism toward the nobles and officials. [Alternatively, he did not quarrel with them out of anger, for his heart—the governing faculty of the soul, as I explained in my commentary on Proverbs—ruled over him, and he restrained his anger. Nevertheless, he contended with them, not through an emotional outburst of anger but from an awakened sense of justice and righteousness.] “Are you acting as creditors, each man toward his brother?” How can one become a creditor who presses his own brother? Is it not written, “If you lend money to My people, you shall not behave toward him as a creditor; you shall not impose interest upon him”? He thereby reminded them of the Torah’s commandments concerning pressing a debtor, charging interest, and returning collateral. And I convened against them: Through his dispute with them, a large gathering of people assembled.

We have purchased: We have redeemed our Jewish brothers from captivity, buying back our brothers who had been sold to the nations, to the extent of our means. There are already many among us whom we have redeemed from slavery. How, then, can you sell your brothers to the nations, forcing us to redeem them as well, so that they will be sold back to us by the nations? Is this to be the result of your actions?

And I said, “It is not good”: Apart from being contrary to the Torah and to justice, it is also not good for you yourselves. Should you not walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the nations, our enemies? Even if you do not fear God and are not scrupulous in observing the Torah’s commandments, you must at least appear to walk and conduct yourselves in the fear of God, so that the nations will not disgrace you by saying that you have neither faith nor religion and that you despise God, thereby subjecting you to reproach.

And also: Do not say that I rebuke you only because I will suffer no loss, since I have not lent them anything. Therefore, he said, “I too, along with my brothers and my servants, have lent them money.” Nevertheless, let us now relinquish this debt and forgive what they owe us. Therefore—

Restore them to them: You too must return their property. This very day: Since this is a year of famine and they are occupied with rebuilding the wall, they have become impoverished and hungry. And the hundred of silver: That is, forgive the loan itself, even if it amounts to one hundred pieces of silver.
And I summoned the priests: He had the priests administer the oath to them, making it more solemn, as it is written, “The priest shall adjure the woman with the oath of the curse.”

I also shook out the fold of my garment: He shook the corner of his garment—the pocket formed by the garment. [The verse “They shall bring your sons in their bosom” may likewise mean “in their pocket”; figuratively, it says that they will carry them as one carries gold and silver in a pocket.] “So may he be shaken out, and so may he remain emptied”: Just as I have shaken out the fold of my garment, so may God shake such a person out of his house—that is, may his house be destroyed and all the fruits of his labor perish. And just as the pocket now remains empty, so may he remain emptied, never again attaining success, even through natural means. And they praised Hashem and acted accordingly: They did it joyfully, as one fulfills a commandment and first recites the blessing over the commandment. Here they fulfilled the commandments of charity and returning collateral. Many great authorities have already debated whether one should recite a blessing when fulfilling commandments of this kind.

Also: That is, not only did he benefit the poor, but he also did not impose a burden upon the wealthy; therefore, they listened to him. Their governors: The letter mem marks the plural—“their governor.”

But the former governors burdened the people: They burdened them with the expenses of their provisions, while the governors who came before me went further and collected taxes from them. He explains that the earlier governors, who did not collect a monetary tax, burdened the people by taking bread and wine, whereas those who followed took money from them. Afterward, forty shekels of silver: That is, another governor took a tax of forty shekels of silver. Alternatively, it means that afterward the governors began taking money.

Moreover: I devoted myself to and assisted in rebuilding the wall. Consequently, we acquired no field, for all my servants were assembled there for the work, and no one was available to perform the agricultural labor. Thus, I had no income at all.

And the Jews: His expenses were considerable because of all those who ate at his table, to the extent that one ox and so forth had to be prepared each day. And between every ten days: Nehemiah “tithed” his days—every tenth day he fasted and drank no wine. Only during the intervening days, when he was not fasting, was every kind of wine supplied in abundance—that is, many different wines, all in plentiful quantities. Nevertheless, although he incurred great expenses without any income, I did not demand the governor’s food allowance.

Remember … concerning this people: The word “concerning” has the sense of “for this people.” Alternatively, Nehemiah means that God should remember this merit not for his own sake, but so that God would apply the merit to this people, for the merit of the righteous protects the people.
Until that time: Until then, they still hoped that they might succeed in stopping the work; afterward, however, they lost their confidence, as stated in verse 16.
In Kephirim: This is the name of a place. We likewise find a city named Chephirah in the territory of Benjamin (Joshua 18:26).
In this manner: He also sent an oral message through his servant that they should meet in Kephirim, while the servant carried a letter indicating that the matter was urgent.

The questions:
(6–7) How could he attempt to frighten Nehemiah with the false accusations that he intended to become king and had appointed prophets to proclaim him king in Judah? Would Nehemiah be afraid of fabricated charges? And the expression “according to these reports” appears to make no sense.

“It is reported among the nations, and Geshem says”: That is, Geshem the Arab says—and it is likewise rumored among the nations—that you are rebuilding the wall because you intend to rebel. The statement “and you are becoming their king” consists of Sanballat’s own words. He means: although the rumor circulating among the nations has no real substance—for people see you building a wall with gates and bars and merely infer that you intend to rebel—nevertheless, Geshem the Arab had already made this accusation when they first sought to build, saying, “Are you rebelling against the king?” (above, 2:19). Nehemiah paid no attention to his words then, and certainly had no reason to do so now, since he was acting with the king’s authorization. Sanballat therefore added: “And you are becoming their king—[this] confirms these reports.” The word “says” at the beginning of the verse applies to both clauses. Your becoming king—something you are doing without the king’s authorization, since he appointed you only as governor and did not authorize you to assume the title of king—confirms and substantiates the reports that you intend to rebel against the king and built the wall for that purpose. He then explains the claim that “you are becoming their king”: “You have also appointed prophets.” As will be explained in verse 12, Tobiah and Sanballat had hired Shemaiah, a false prophet, to prophesy that there would be a king in Jerusalem and that Nehemiah would be that king. He prophesied to Nehemiah that he would reign. [This prophecy by itself would not imply rebellion, because it might be fulfilled with the Persian king’s permission, by his appointing Nehemiah as king, just as many kings ruled under the authority of the Persian monarchs.] They hired the prophets so that, when necessary, they could claim that Nehemiah himself had hired them to deliver this prophecy, which would constitute rebellion. On this basis, Sanballat presented apparent proof that Nehemiah intended to rebel: You have appointed and hired prophets to proclaim that you will be king in Judah. [It was true that the false prophets had prophesied this, though they had actually been hired by Judah’s enemies.] “And now it will be reported to the king”—this will cause even your rebuilding of the wall to be regarded as an act of rebellion. “Therefore, come, and let us take counsel together” about how you can save yourself.

The questions:
(8–9) Why did Nehemiah need to send him a response saying that he had invented these accusations, when they were plainly false? What is the meaning of “for they all sought to frighten us,” and what does this add to the account?

And I sent: He replied that this claim—that I appointed prophets—never happened, for you are inventing it out of your own heart. Your invitation that I should consult with you, as though you were my friends seeking to strengthen my hand, is likewise false. For until now, all of them—that is, all of Judah’s enemies, including you—have sought to frighten us, saying, “Their hands will become weak in the work.” How, then, have you suddenly changed from an enemy into a friend who wishes to strengthen my hand?

The questions:
(10–13) If Shemaiah said this in God’s name, how did Nehemiah recognize that God had not sent him? Moreover, the text does not mention that he presented his words as a prophecy; had he done so, it should have said, “Thus says Hashem: Hide yourself within the Temple.” What is the meaning of the expression “for he spoke the prophecy”? It should have said, “He spoke prophetically.” And what is the meaning of the phrase “because he was hired,” which appears entirely incomprehensible?

And I came to the house of Shemaiah: Nehemiah had resolved to investigate the prophecy that Shemaiah had pronounced concerning him—that he would become king in Judah—and therefore went to Shemaiah’s house. [For he was confined by illness and could not be summoned to Nehemiah.] Nehemiah went to investigate and inquire into the matter. And he said, “Let us meet in the House of God”: Shemaiah did not say this as a prophecy. Rather, he told Nehemiah that he had learned through informants that Judah’s enemies were coming to kill him and intended to murder him that very night. He therefore advised Nehemiah to accompany him into the Sanctuary and remain locked inside throughout the night, because the Sanctuary’s doors were closed, whereas the city’s gates were open.

And I said to him: He replied that he would not do this for two reasons. First, it would make him appear fearful and fainthearted, which was unbecoming a man of his position. Thus he said, “Should a man such as I flee?” Second, “Who such as I could enter the Sanctuary and live?” After all, I am not a priest, and a non-priest may not approach the sacred place.

And I recognized: From this I recognized that God had not sent him—that is, that he was a false prophet—for he was the one who had spoken the prophecy concerning me, namely, the prophecy mentioned above that I would become king over Israel. Until then, I had been uncertain whether it might be a true prophecy; now, however, I recognized that God had not sent him, but that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. They had hired him both to prophesy that Nehemiah would become king over Israel and to advise him to enter the Sanctuary. [Nehemiah now recognized this because Shemaiah’s present advice contradicted his earlier prophecy. If God had truly declared that Nehemiah would become king over Israel, how could his enemies kill him, forcing him to hide from them in the Sanctuary? On the contrary, Shemaiah should have told him, “Do not fear, for the word of God will not return unfulfilled, and you will surely reign.” From this contradiction, Nehemiah recognized that God had not sent him; rather, Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him for each of these two acts.]

In order that: The verse explains why they hired Shemaiah to prophesy that Nehemiah would reign over Israel. This is the meaning of “in order that he might appear to have been hired”: they intended to accuse Nehemiah by claiming that Shemaiah had been hired by him to utter this prophecy, as Sanballat had alleged, “You have also appointed prophets to proclaim concerning you, ‘There is a king.’” Why, then, did they hire him to advise Nehemiah to flee into the Sanctuary? “In order that I would become afraid and act accordingly.” They would thereby gain two advantages: first, “and I would sin” and be punished for this transgression; second, “and they would have grounds for an evil report, in order” to reproach me for having desecrated God’s Sanctuary.

Remember, O my God, Tobiah according to these deeds of his: That is, for hiring false prophets against Nehemiah. And also Noadiah the prophetess: This refers to Shemaiah and Noadiah, both of whom were hired to prophesy that Nehemiah would become king, as well as to the other prophets who were hired to cast terror and fear upon him.
On the twenty-fifth: This was in the same year in which Nehemiah came up from Shushan, and the work was completed after fifty-two days.

And they lost their confidence: For they knew that this work had been accomplished by our God. They saw that it had succeeded through Divine Providence; therefore, it was completed in so few days, and they had been unable to stop the work.

The questions:
(17) How is the statement “Moreover, in those days” connected with the preceding statement that their enemies had lost their confidence?

Moreover, in those days: This introduces what Nehemiah relates in the following chapter: that he appointed his brother over the walls of Jerusalem and ordered the city to remain guarded even afterward. Although the fear of God had fallen upon the surrounding nations, he still faced stumbling blocks among the Israelites themselves, who exchanged letters with Tobiah, for they were allied with him for two reasons. First, he was related by marriage to Shecaniah and Meshullam, who were prominent and honored officials. Second, they spoke favorably of him and regarded him as a good and upright man. Consequently, they also conveyed Nehemiah’s words and secrets to Tobiah, who thus had spies among the Israelites. He also sent letters to frighten me. Nehemiah therefore remained on guard against him and ordered increased vigilance even after the wall had been built, although he no longer feared the surrounding nations.
And they were appointed: Until then, the Levites had been occupied with rebuilding the wall; now they were assigned to their duties of guarding it.

And he feared God more than most: As the Sages said, “Would that the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood.” Most people fear the public and will refrain from acting against their wishes, even when their wishes conflict with the word of God. Here, however, an official was needed who would fear no man. Since many prominent officials were allied with Tobiah, as explained above, Nehemiah chose Hanani, who would not be intimidated by them.

They shall not be opened: This was to prevent enemies plotting harm from entering the city. And while the guards are still standing there, they shall keep the doors shut: The gateways were double. There was a large outer gate, and inside it was another gate fitted with small doors through which individuals could enter. Nehemiah commanded that even when the gates were opened, the guard should keep hold of these doors and keep them closed rather than leaving them open. In this way, he could observe every person entering and prevent anyone from entering without permission. And appoint: He also commanded that the watches guarding the city be stationed each at his own post. A man assigned to one watch was not to be exchanged with someone from another, for otherwise the city would not be guarded properly. Anyone whose house was near the wall was to stand guard opposite his own house.

The questions:
(4–5) What did Nehemiah intend by mentioning here that the city was large, that its houses had not been built, and that he resolved to register the people by genealogy? Moreover, the genealogical record itself contains several discrepancies between the figures given here and those recorded in the Book of Ezra; likewise, the accounts of the donations made by the officials and the people contradict one another.

And the city: This introduces what follows. Seeing that the city’s population was small, Nehemiah wished to settle some of the Israelites there, as he later did (11:1). Since its houses had not been built, however, he realized that people would be unwilling to settle in a city lacking proper dwellings unless lots were cast to determine who would live there, as indeed occurred. He therefore needed to know which families had returned to the Land of Israel, so that each family could contribute residents in proportion to its number of men. Consequently, he assembled them to be registered by genealogy. This is the meaning of the following verse.

And my God put it into my heart: God placed in his heart the plan to assemble them for registration by genealogy. While investigating the matter, he found the genealogical record of those who had returned at the beginning and found it written down. This is the record contained in Ezra, chapter 2. However, there are several differences between the version here and that in Ezra. We have already discussed them there, and in the commentary on this chapter you will find the entire explanation; there is no need to repeat it.

And some of the heads of the ancestral houses: This account of the donations also differs from that in Ezra. There, the gold amounted to sixty-one thousand darics and was donated by the heads of the ancestral houses, whereas here the heads of the ancestral houses donated only twenty thousand and the people gave another twenty thousand. There, the heads of the ancestral houses donated five thousand minas of silver, whereas here they gave two thousand two hundred minas and the remainder of the people gave two thousand. There, the heads of the ancestral houses donated one hundred priestly garments, whereas here they donated no garments, but the people donated sixty-seven. Moreover, the Tirshatha’s donation is mentioned here but not there. If we assume that Nehemiah also returned in the first migration—and afterward went back and came a second time, as appears from verse 65, “The Tirshatha said to them”—then it may be suggested that they donated on two separate occasions. In particular, according to what I explained in Ezra, chapter 2—that Ezra’s account enumerates those who came from Babylonia, whereas the present account enumerates those from the surrounding province who were added to them—it may be that they made a second donation afterward. On that occasion, the Tirshatha and the people also donated, while the leaders donated a second time; alternatively, new heads of ancestral houses had been added, and this was recorded in the genealogical document Nehemiah found. Another possibility is that the second donation was made when Nehemiah arrived in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, and he added it to this scroll because he knew that the first donation had already been recorded in the Book of Ezra, which was written before his own book.

And the priests settled … and the seventh month arrived: This same wording also appears at the end of the genealogical scroll in Ezra. There, however, it leads into the account of the building of the altar, whereas here it leads into the account of the public reading of the Torah. Opinions therefore differ concerning its interpretation. Some say that this passage continues the account of the events surrounding the first return, in the days of Cyrus. According to this view, the statement in verse 5, “I found the genealogical record and found written in it,” extends through the end of the chapter, meaning that Nehemiah found this entire account written in the genealogical record. It would then follow that Ezra returned twice: the first time, in the days of Cyrus, together with Zerubbabel. Nehemiah likewise returned at that time, as indicated below (8:9): “Nehemiah, who was the Tirshatha, said,” and in 10:2: “Among those who signed were Nehemiah the Tirshatha, son of Hacaliah.” Ezra 2:2, 63 likewise appears to indicate that Nehemiah accompanied Zerubbabel. Similarly, Nehemiah 12:1 lists Ezra among those who returned with Zerubbabel, and it may refer to Ezra the Scribe. This would also resolve the statement in Ezra 3:4, “They celebrated the Feast of Sukkot as prescribed,” so that it would not contradict the statement in this book (8:17). Others maintain that this event occurred in Nehemiah’s time, after the wall had been rebuilt. Since the genealogical scroll ended with the statement, “The seventh month arrived, and the people assembled,” and the same thing now occurred, Nehemiah concluded the record with that verse and used it to introduce the events of his own time. According to this view, the statement in Ezra that “they celebrated the Feast of Sukkot” means that they observed it with Hallel, rejoicing, pilgrimage offerings, festival peace-offerings, and the four species, although they did not then fulfill the commandment of dwelling in a sukkah properly. In particular, the verse there is primarily concerned with the festival sacrifices, as it says, “They celebrated the Feast of Sukkot as prescribed, with the daily burnt offerings in the proper number, according to the ordinance,” for the passage concerns the offerings upon the altar. Judging from the sequence of the verses, this second opinion is more convincing.

The Torah: The verse does not say “the Book of the Torah,” as it does afterward when it says, “They read from it”—that is, from the book. This broader expression includes the fact that they also explained the orally transmitted Torah, which is not written in the book. Thus it says, “before the assembly, from man to woman”—the plain teachings were read before them—“and all who could understand what they heard” refers to the sages, before whom the teachings and mysteries of the Oral Torah were expounded.

And they stood beside him: There were seven on each side, with Ezra counted among those on the right. According to the Sages in Megillah 23a, however, there were six on each side apart from Ezra, and “Zechariah Meshullam” is the name of a single person. Yet Ezra 8:16 says, “and Zechariah and Meshullam, the leaders,” and this requires further examination.
Above all the people: The tower was a raised platform. They stood: They ceased speaking (Sotah 39a).

With the raising of their hands: That is, by lifting their hands. According to Ibn Ezra, the word derives from a verb with a doubled root letter, while the letter mem serves to form the noun, as in morekh (“faintness”). See what I wrote in HaTorah VehaMitzvah, Beḥukkotai, section 63.

From the book, from the Torah of God: This means both from the written book—the Written Torah—and from the Torah of God transmitted orally. For this reason, the preposition bet is repeated before each phrase. Concerning “from the book,” the verse says “distinctly,” which the Sages interpreted as referring to translation: they translated it into the language of the people. Corresponding to “the Torah of God,” it says, “and they gave the sense,” meaning that they taught the people the Oral Torah. How the Oral Torah is derived from the Written Torah is expressed by “and they caused them to understand the reading.” The Sages (Nedarim 37b; Megillah 3a) explained: “They gave the sense” refers to the division into verses, while “they caused them to understand the reading” refers to the Masoretic tradition. The division of the verses, the punctuation of the cantillation marks, and the proper pronunciation are all part of the Oral Torah—for example, whether to read baḥelev immo (“in its mother’s fat”) or baḥalav immo (“in its mother’s milk”), and whether to pronounce zekher Amalek or zeikher Amalek. The same applies to the five verses whose syntactic division cannot be conclusively determined, as the Sages explained.

For they were weeping: It may be explained that Ezra read before them the Torah portion appropriate to that day and taught them that it was a Day of Judgment. They therefore wept from fear of the judgment and also wished to fast. In response to their desire to fast, he told them, “Go, eat rich foods,” and in response to their weeping, “Do not grieve.” As the Midrash explains, when Israel faces judgment, they celebrate a festival because they trust that God will render a favorable judgment for them. This is the meaning of “for the joy of Hashem is your strength”: through this joy, you demonstrate that your strength lies in God and that He will bestow His kindness upon you. The term ḥedvah specifically denotes spiritual joy. This joy is your strength—the soul’s joy in cleaving to God gives it strength, for God is its strength and its stronghold.

Be still, for the day is holy: Earlier, in verse 9, he said, “This day is holy to Hashem your God.” As the Sages taught, “Divide it—half for Hashem and half for yourselves.” There he referred to the first half of the day, which they had consecrated to God. Now, when he instructed them to return home and eat rich foods, the Levites added that the second half of the day was also holy, because they would fulfill the commandment of rejoicing on the festival. Therefore, they said simply, “The day is holy.”

For they understood: They understood that it was a commandment both to rejoice and to bring joy to the poor, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. They therefore sent portions of food and celebrated with great joy, so that all the people—poor and wealthy alike—would rejoice together.

That the children of Israel should dwell in booths during the festival: This is exceedingly puzzling, for it would imply that Israel had not observed the commandment of sukkah from the days of Joshua until then, as stated below: “The children of Israel had not done so since the days of Joshua son of Nun.” The Sages likewise expressed astonishment at this in Arakhin 32b. It appears, however, in light of the Rema’s ruling in Orach Chayim 637 that one may not build a sukkah in the public domain, that the matter can be explained as follows: since we maintain that Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, no true private domain existed there. Just as houses in Jerusalem could not be rented out because they did not belong to their occupants, so too it was impossible to build sukkot there. When, in Ezra’s time, the Israelites acquired the Land of Israel anew through possession and sanctified it, the court stipulated that sukkot could be built in Jerusalem and in other public domains. Thus the Tosefta (Bava Kamma, chapter 6) states that one of the court’s stipulations was that people may roof sukkot in the public domain. This means that Ezra’s court enacted this stipulation at that time; otherwise, they could not have built sukkot in Jerusalem. The verse explicitly states that they built them in the courtyards of the House of God and in the square of the Water Gate, which was literally a public domain. The Tosefta refers specifically to the Land of Israel, where this stipulation was enacted by Ezra’s court when they sanctified the land; no such stipulation was enacted outside the Land, especially in places belonging to non-Jews, as the Magen Avraham discusses there. Joshua could likewise have enacted such an ordinance when he sanctified the land for the first time, since the court then had authority to apportion the land on the condition that the place occupied by a sukkah would always become a private domain. Joshua did not do so. Therefore, from his time until Ezra’s, the children of Israel “had not done so”—meaning that they had not dwelled in sukkot constructed in the public domain. Even in the days of David and Solomon, sukkot were not built in Jerusalem for the reason stated above: Jerusalem had not been divided among the tribes. The words “that they should proclaim and circulate an announcement throughout all their cities” mean that the people were to be informed that in the other cities as well, they could build sukkot in the public domain. We can now understand the teaching in Arakhin that the statement “this had not been done since the days of Joshua son of Nun” means that Ezra sanctified the land a second time. How is this conclusion derived from the words “they had not done so since the days of Joshua”? The very comparison demonstrates that Ezra sanctified the land anew and therefore possessed the authority to enact conditions just as Joshua had in his time. From this, the Gemara there proves that the first sanctification did not sanctify the land permanently.

And bring olive branches: The Sages explained in tractate Sukkah that olive branches and branches of the oil tree were intended for roofing the sukkah; myrtle and palm branches were for the lulav; and branches of a thick-leaved tree refer to the wild myrtle, which was used for roofing. Although the verse’s primary purpose was not to command them concerning the four species—for if it were, it should also have mentioned the fruit of the citron tree and willows of the brook—there were sages among them who followed Rabbi Judah’s interpretation that a sukkah may be made only from the four species, as stated in Sukkah 36b. Ezra therefore taught them that they could bring myrtle and palm branches, which they would be gathering in any event for the commandment of the four species, but that they should also bring olive branches and branches of the oil tree—the latter being a non-fruit-bearing tree, as in “wood of the oil tree” (I Kings 6:23). This would prevent them from establishing as law, through an inference from minor to major, that the sukkah’s roofing must consist of the four species. Thus the verse says, “to make sukkot as it is written”—meaning that we should not derive through such an inference that only the four species may be used, but should follow the law as it is written.

And the entire assembly made them: This accords with what was explained above: they built the sukkot in the public domain, which served as a communal sukkah, for the court had now enacted a stipulation permitting this. Therefore, they dwelled in the sukkot, whereas previously many had not dwelled in sukkot because they had no private domain in which to build one.
And on the twenty-fourth day: They could not fast on the twenty-third, because it was the day following the festival, on which fasting is prohibited.

From all foreigners: That is, from foreign wives. After separating from them at the time of Ezra’s return, they later stumbled in this matter a second time. According to the interpretation that this event occurred at the time of Zerubbabel’s return, the practice continued to spread until Ezra corrected it.

And the Levites said: This is the structure of the prayer: first, it recounts how God chose Abraham and his descendants to be His treasured people and made a covenant with him to give him and his descendants the land suited to this purpose (verses 7–8); how He kept His covenant by bringing them out of Egypt and sustaining them in the wilderness (verses 9–15); how, although they rebelled against Him, He did not withdraw His word but brought them into the land (verses 15–25); and how they sinned and provoked Him there, while He dealt with them for many years according to His mercy, until He delivered them into the hands of the peoples of the lands (verses 26–30). Since throughout all this He did not abandon them, His Providence remained upon them, and He remains prepared to preserve His covenant forever, they ask Him to remember all the hardships they endured during their exile. They, in turn, will correct the sins of their ancestors by making a covenant to observe His laws and commandments (verses 31–37; 10:1). “Arise” is a command that everyone should bless God, who is blessed both in this world and in the eternal world that will follow it. After instructing the people to bless God, the speaker turns toward God and says: They will bless Your glorious name. That is, in Your very essence, You are exalted and raised beyond every blessing and praise, for no one can apprehend You in order to praise You, nor can anyone comprehend the emanation proceeding from Your essence so as to bless You on that basis. You are utterly hidden, elevated beyond every blessing and praise. What they can bless is only Your glorious name—the name by which You have become known through the glory revealed in the creation You made, through which Your glory and kingship became manifest. It is this name that they will bless, not Your essence, for—

You are exalted above all blessing and praise; You alone are Hashem: You alone, in Your very essence, are exalted and raised beyond every blessing and praise. After this introduction, the prayer explains the words “They shall bless Your glorious name.” The glorious name through which God becomes known to His creatures is revealed through three things. First, through creation; thus it says, “You made the heavens,” and so forth—that is, You created both the upper and lower realms. Second, through the preservation of creation and its continuous governance; thus it says, “And You give life to them all.” You are unlike any other maker, whose work continues to exist independently after he has made it. The entire creation possesses existence and life only through You, for You are the soul that gives life to all reality. Although it appears that the world is governed through the heavenly host and the order of the celestial system, nevertheless, “the host of heaven bows down to You,” for You govern them, grant them their power, and rule over them all.

You: Third, Your glorious name becomes known through miraculous providential governance. This does not operate according to the established order of the heavenly system, but according to the deeds of the holy ones upon earth—the uniquely chosen individuals upon whom this wondrous Providence rests, overturning nature and performing miracles for those who fear God. This form of Providence began with Abraham. Thus it says, “You are Hashem God who chose Abram”—God chose him to become the vehicle for miraculous governance—“and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans.” At that time, You first suspended nature for his sake, and he was saved from the fiery furnace. Afterward, “You gave him the name Abraham,” as a sign that he would become the father of a multitude of nations, and that his descendants would likewise be a treasured people, worthy of attachment to the Divine, with God’s presence dwelling among them.

And You found: After Abraham had withstood all the trials through which he was tested, his heart was found faithful to his God. Therefore, You made a covenant with him to give him the land of the Canaanite, the land uniquely suited to providential and miraculous governance, and to give it to his descendants. The covenant was to give it to Abraham through Divine designation and promise, and to give it to his descendants by bringing them there to inherit it, as stated, “To you I will give it, and to your descendants forever.” The prayer now begins to recount how God fulfilled His covenant, as it says, “And You fulfilled Your words.” There was no injustice in taking the land from the Canaanites, for “You are righteous,” as it is written, “Because of the wickedness of these nations, Hashem drives them out before you.”

And You saw: The prayer explains how God fulfilled His words. Their sojourn in Egypt was a necessary preparation for inheriting the land, as stated, “Your descendants will be strangers,” for Egypt was the iron furnace in which they were refined and tested, so that they would become worthy of miraculous Providence cleaving to them. Then “You saw their affliction.” The clauses correspond to one another: “You saw the affliction of our ancestors,” and therefore “You performed signs and wonders”; “You heard their cry at the Red Sea,” and therefore “You divided the sea before them.” Because You saw the affliction of our ancestors—therefore—

And You performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh: This was for two reasons. First, as punishment for the Egyptians’ mistreatment of Israel. Although the exile occurred through God’s decree—“They shall enslave and afflict them”—God knew that the Egyptians did not afflict them in order to fulfill that decree. Rather, “You knew that they had acted presumptuously against them”: they deliberately increased Israel’s suffering and oppression, not because of God’s word but from the wickedness of their own hearts. [Thus God said, “And I will also judge the nation whom they shall serve”—meaning that He would judge whether they had enslaved Israel because of His decree or from the malice of their own hearts.] The second reason was: “And You made a name for Yourself, as it is this day.” The signs and wonders were intended to cause people to recognize God’s name and glory, as it is written: “Come to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart … so that I may place these signs of Mine in his midst,” corresponding to the first reason; and “so that you may recount … and you shall know that I am Hashem,” corresponding to the second.

And the sea: You heard their cry at the Red Sea, and You divided the sea before them for two purposes: first, to save them, so that they could pass through the sea on dry land; and second, to drown their enemies—“You cast their pursuers into the depths.”

And with the pillar: The prayer now recounts how, after they left Egypt, Israel became God’s treasured people: “Their King passed before them, with Hashem at their head.” First, He dwelled in their midst to show them the way, as it says, “You guided them by a pillar of cloud.” Thus it is written, “They have heard that You, Hashem, are in the midst of this people, that Your cloud stands over them, and that You go before them by day in a pillar of cloud,” and so forth. This was the sign that God dwelled among them with the cloud of His glory.

Second, “You descended upon Mount Sinai”: God’s own glory was then revealed to them in order to give them His Torah. “And You gave them”: While they were still at Mount Sinai, He gave them the Ten Commandments and the entire passage through the end of Mishpatim. There He commanded Moses concerning ordinances governing relations between one person and another; a Torah of truth concerning matters of faith; statutes, such as “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk”; and good commandments, such as “If you lend money,” and similar laws.

And the Sabbath: The Sabbath was commanded in the Ten Commandments and again at the end of the portion of Mishpatim. The verse says, “You made known to them,” because through the Sabbath God revealed to them the fundamental principles of faith concerning the creation of the world and taught them that they are governed through Divine Providence. For this reason, the commandment of the Sabbath was given, as I have explained elsewhere. And commandments: That is, afterward You taught them commandments, statutes, and Torah throughout the period in which they remained in the wilderness of Sinai, until they encamped in the wilderness of Paran. During that time, You gave them all the commandments recorded in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers through the portion of Sh’laḥ.

And bread: He also watched over them providentially, providing all their needs in the wilderness. And You told them to enter and possess the land: At that time, He instructed them to go and take possession of the land, as it is written, “I said to you: You have come to the mountain of the Amorites … Go up and possess it” (Deuteronomy 1:20–21).

But they: They acted presumptuously and said, “Let us send men ahead of us.” Afterward, they refused to listen. Although Moses told them, “Do not be terrified and do not fear them; Hashem will fight for you, just as He did for you in Egypt,” they did not remember Your wonders, and they appointed a leader, as they said, “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt.” Nevertheless, You are a God of forgiveness, and so forth.

Even when: This was not their first sin, for they had already sinned by making the Golden Calf, at which time they likewise deserved destruction. Nevertheless, in Your abundant mercy You did not abandon them. Although they wandered in the wilderness for forty years, they still had the pillars of fire and cloud, the spirit of prophecy resting upon Moses to instruct them, as well as the manna and the well. Throughout those forty years, You sustained them and provided all their needs, even while they remained under Divine displeasure because of their sin.

And You gave them: You further gave them the lands of Sihon and Og, which You had not promised to the Patriarchs at all. And You apportioned them to a region: You assigned two and a half tribes a separate region and territory beyond the Jordan. Because You had multiplied their children and they required a spacious land, You expanded the land’s boundaries. And You brought them into the land and fulfilled the covenant You had made with Abraham. The prayer has thus recounted how God kept His covenant.

And the children entered the Land of Israel, and they inherited the land. And You subdued: The prayer explains how they took possession of the land. Some nations You subdued before them: the Girgashites, who withdrew and departed, and the Hivites, who made peace with them, submitted, and did not fight.
