As for the other nations that fought against them, You delivered them into their hands, and they conquered them in battle—both the peoples and their kings—to do with them as they wished, removing them from the face of the earth.

And they captured: This corresponds to the language of the Torah (Deuteronomy 6:10–11): “When Hashem brings you into the land that He swore to your ancestors … great cities that you did not build.” “And they inherited houses” corresponds to “houses filled with every good thing that you did not fill”; “cisterns” to “hewn cisterns that you did not hew”; “vineyards” to “vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant”; and “they ate” to “you shall eat and be satisfied.” There the Torah continues, “Take care lest you forget Hashem,” and therefore the prayer next says—
And they rebelled: Afterward, they forgot Hashem. At first, they disobeyed His word, and later they rebelled completely, casting Your Torah behind their backs, and so forth.

And You delivered them: This occurred in the days of the Judges, as stated in Judges 2:14. The prayer distinguishes two stages. At first, it says that God delivered them into the hands of their oppressors, and afterward into the hands of their enemies. An “oppressor” is one who actively causes distress, whereas an “enemy” is one who harbors hatred in his heart. A person may be an oppressor without being an enemy, inflicting harm for his own benefit rather than from hatred. The second time, God delivered them into the hands of their enemies, who were harsher than their oppressors and subjugated them in exile even without needing to besiege them. And they ruled over them: This domination was more severe than what was stated on the first occasion, “and they oppressed them.” Moreover, concerning the first occasion, it says, “You gave them saviors who saved them,” whereas concerning the second, it says merely, “You delivered them.” Salvation means being saved completely and defeating the enemy, as occurred through deliverers such as Ehud and Deborah. On the second occasion, however, God merely rescued them from being destroyed by the enemy, without granting them a complete victory. Therefore, on the first occasion it says, “according to Your abundant mercies,” while on the second it says only, “according to Your mercy,” without describing the mercy as abundant or great, because the deliverance was limited. This occurred many times, throughout the entire period of the Judges.

And You warned them: Later, however, during the period of the kings, they began to sin continually, from the days of Jeroboam onward. You warned them, yet they acted presumptuously—for presumption means defying God openly and high-handedly. They did not obey Your commandments governing the relationship between man and God. They also sinned against Your ordinances, which a person shall perform and live by them—the laws sustaining an orderly society. They presented a rebellious shoulder to words of rebuke, and even when You punished them, they stiffened their necks.

And You prolonged: This continued for many years. And You warned them: Through the prophets, God then testified concerning the decree He had issued against them. These were the prophets who arose from the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, onward, all of whom prophesied. And You bore with them: This continued for many years. And You warned them: Through the prophets, You then testified concerning the decree You had issued against them. These were the prophets who arose from the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, onward, all of whom prophesied concerning the exile. But they did not listen, and therefore You delivered them into the hands of the peoples of the lands, beginning with the exile of the Ten Tribes by Assyria and continuing through the exile of Judah and Benjamin.

And in Your mercy: Despite everything, You had compassion upon them and did not destroy them completely. God watched over them “through the windows” and accompanied them into the land of their exile to protect them, as it is written, “Yet even then, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them … to destroy them utterly and break My covenant with them.” For He still preserves the covenant and kindness that He promised to the Patriarchs, as it says there, “I will remember My covenant with Jacob,” and so forth.

And now, our God: Since You still keep the covenant and kindness, as it is written, “I will remember My covenant with Jacob,” it follows that Your not abandoning them results from Your faithfulness to the covenant. [For this reason, the prayer added the titles “mighty and awesome,” which Jeremiah had omitted and which the Men of the Great Assembly restored, as the Sages explained. They saw that even during exile God displays His might, awesomeness, and particular Providence. Although His Providence operates in a veiled and hidden manner on a lower level, these themselves are manifestations of His mighty deeds, as I have explained elsewhere.] Let it not seem insignificant: Since the covenant remains in force and the exile serves only to atone for iniquity and bring transgression to an end, we have already received from God more than enough suffering, from the days of the kings of Assyria, when the exiles began, until this very day.

And You are righteous: Nevertheless, You were righteous in punishing us. This is true first from our own perspective: in all that has come upon us, we have acted wickedly. We continued to act wickedly despite all the suffering and affliction that befell us. Although You acted faithfully and the punishment was just, we did not take it to heart and repent, but continued acting wickedly even in our exile. And it is also true from the perspective of our ancestors, for—

And our kings: In the earlier period, in the days of our ancestors, when we had kings and officials, our kings, our officials, and all our ancestors did not heed Your commandments. They were not then suffering siege or distress, yet they did not serve You in their kingdom or amid Your abundant goodness. Thus we withstood neither the test of prosperity nor the test of poverty: we rebelled against God both in times of success and in days of affliction. [The expression “and our kings” means, “You are righteous with regard to our kings”; the particle et has the same meaning as im, “with” or “regarding.”]

Behold: Nehemiah now concludes his prayer by saying: We wish to correct the sin of our ancestors and turn away God’s wrath. Whereas our ancestors did not serve You despite their abundant prosperity and the good land they possessed, we will serve You even amid poverty and deprivation. Although we are slaves, and as for the land—we are slaves upon it, and its produce yields an increase—the word denotes interest, as in “Woe to him who increases what is not his.” That is, we pay interest and usury for the land to kings who rule over our bodies and our livestock, until we are in great distress. Nevertheless, we make a firm covenant and undertake to observe the Torah. In this way, we will correct the sin of our ancestors, who did not serve You when they lived in the land and possessed every good thing.

And despite all this, although we are in distress, we make a firm covenant—that is, a faithful and enduring covenant, in contrast to our ancestors, who did not serve God despite possessing abundance. And upon the sealed document: This refers to the document upon which they placed their signatures. It may be that their custom, whenever recording a binding agreement, was to write it in two documents: one open document and one sealed document, as described in Jeremiah 32:11, 14. The open document was signed on the inside, while the sealed document was signed on the outside, as the Sages said: “A plain bill has its witnesses inside; a folded bill has its witnesses outside.” The order of signatures was first the priests, then the Levites, and finally the officials. This was the order in the open document. In the sealed document, however, the signed portions were folded outward, reversing the order so that those who had signed last appeared first: first the officials, then the Levites, and then the priests. Thus, when the verse says, “And upon the sealed document,” meaning the sealed document, the order was “our officials, our Levites, and our priests.”

And among those who signed: This refers to the open document, where the signatories appeared in their original order: first the priests, then the Levites, and afterward the leaders of the people. If you count them, you will find that eighty-three people signed. They correspond to the seventy members of the Sanhedrin and the thirteen Temple officials enumerated by Maimonides in chapter 4 of the Laws of the Temple Vessels, apart from the High Priest, who is not mentioned among the signatories: the deputy High Priest, two katikolin, seven amarkalin, and three treasurers.

And the rest: That is, the rest of the people who did not sign the document supported their brethren and consented to the oath. And everyone who had separated himself: This refers to the converts. Everyone who knew and understood: Both their wives, who lacked understanding, and everyone who possessed knowledge and understanding—all of them supported their brethren and accepted the oath.
That we would not give: Even though they were not members of the seven Canaanite nations.

And the peoples of the land: They accepted upon themselves the prohibition against buying and selling on the Sabbath, which is not explicitly stated in the Torah. And we would leave the seventh year untended: This excludes the opinion that the Sabbatical year does not apply when the Jubilee does not apply, since the Jubilee applies only when all the land’s inhabitants dwell upon it.

One-third of a shekel: According to the commentators, this was in addition to the half-shekel. See I Kings 7:26, for the coinage had changed by that time, and one-third of the later shekel was equivalent to one-half of the earlier shekel, as stated in Ezekiel 45:12.

For the continual burnt offering, and for the burnt offerings of the Sabbaths, the New Moons, and the festivals, and for the sacred offerings: Such as the Omer offering, the lambs of Shavuot, and the two loaves. And for the sin offerings: The goats offered on the New Moons and festivals.
And we cast lots: As the Sages explained in tractate Ta’anit.

And to bring the first fruits of our soil: Wheat and barley. And the first fruits of every fruit of every tree: Grapes, figs, pomegranates, and so forth. Rashi writes that the obligation to bring the first fruits of every tree is rabbinic. This is puzzling, because the Jerusalem Talmud in tractate Bikkurim states that first fruits brought from species other than the seven species do not become consecrated. It therefore appears that, since the Torah establishes no fixed quantity for first fruits, they undertook to bring a fitting gift to the House of God—one-sixtieth of the produce—in accordance with the rabbinic enactment.

And the firstborn of our sons and our animals: This refers to the firstborn of non-kosher animals, whose redemption payment does not have to be brought to the House of God. And the firstborn of our cattle, to bring to the House of our God: These were brought there to be offered as sacrifices.

And the first portion: This is entirely consistent with Maimonides’ opinion that in the days of Ezra, the obligations of ḥallah, terumah, and tithes applied only by rabbinic law, as he states at the end of chapter 1 of the Laws of Terumot. Accordingly, everything they accepted upon themselves here was rabbinic in origin. According to Raavad, however, terumah was a Torah obligation while only ḥallah was rabbinic. It may therefore be explained that they accepted the obligation of separating terumah from other fruits, as implied by “the fruit of every tree,” since according to his view (Laws of Tithes 1:9), only grain, wine, and oil are obligated by Torah law. Thus it says, “and the tithe of our soil,” meaning from everything that grows from the soil. And they, the Levites, shall receive the tithes: The Levites are the ones who collect the tithe in all the cities of our labor, wherever agricultural work is performed in the fields.

And the priest shall be with the Levites: According to the Sages, the Levites were penalized at that time by allowing the priests also to receive the first tithe (see Yevamot 86b and Chullin 131b). That is, the priests were permitted to take the tithe as well, while the tithe of the tithe still had to be given to the priests even from produce received by a Levite.

And they dwelled: The text now relates how Nehemiah completed the plan he had conceived—to register the people by genealogy so that members of every family could be settled in Jerusalem and the city would not remain desolate, as explained above (7:4–5). After the people undertook to support the priests and the House of God, the leaders remained in Jerusalem, while the rest of the people cast lots and set aside a tithe of the population to live there as well.

And the people blessed: In addition, many volunteered even though the lot had not fallen upon them, and the people blessed them for their generosity of spirit, because living in large cities is difficult, as the Sages taught concerning this.

And these: This refers to those listed below. And in the cities of Judah: The remainder of the people continued living in the cities of Judah, each man on his ancestral property in their cities, where their forefathers had lived before the exile.

And in Jerusalem they dwelled: You should know that the matters recorded here also appear in I Chronicles, chapter 9, but with many variations and apparent contradictions between the two versions. The commentators have offered strange explanations for them; however, all these rough places become level when understood in light of what I have explained: the Book of Ezra is a continuation and completion of Chronicles. Ezra the Scribe joined the Book of Ezra to Chronicles, which he had written previously, and Nehemiah then completed the Book of Ezra. I have already explained that the differences between Chronicles and the earlier biblical books arise because, when Ezra composed Chronicles, he repeated material from the earlier books in order to explain it or add a detail not mentioned there. Thus, his accounts are generally not mere repetitions of the earlier narratives but supplements to them. With God’s help, this principle has enabled me to resolve most of the questions and apparent contradictions in Chronicles. Similarly, when Nehemiah repeated here material that Ezra had already written in Chronicles, he did not merely copy the earlier account but added information that had not been recorded there. Thus, Nehemiah begins, “These are the heads of the province who dwelled in Jerusalem”—these are Nehemiah’s own words. From that point onward, he quotes Ezra’s wording from Chronicles: “And in the cities of Judah they dwelled … and in Jerusalem they dwelled,” thereby informing us that he is quoting the language of Chronicles. There, Ezra wrote, “Some of the descendants of Judah, some of the descendants of Benjamin, and some of the descendants of Ephraim and Manasseh.” Nehemiah omitted this because it had already been recorded there. Here, however, he writes, “Of the descendants of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah,” and so forth, whereas Chronicles says, “Uthai son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, of the descendants of Perez son of Judah.” Ezra did not record the entire genealogical chain back to Perez, but listed only four generations between Uthai and Perez, omitting the others. Nehemiah found additional distinguished individuals in the genealogical record and inserted two notable ancestors between Athaiah and Amariah—the latter being the Imri mentioned there. Above Amariah, he likewise added Benjamin, who was also a distinguished person, while continuing to omit the remaining ancestors who were not notable figures.

And Maaseiah: In Chronicles (there, verse 5), it says, “And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn and his sons.” This Asaiah is the Maaseiah mentioned here. Nehemiah found the genealogical record and added clarification to Ezra’s account. The “Shilonite” was a distinguished descendant of Perez who served as the head of the family.

All the descendants of Perez: Chronicles further states, “And of the descendants of Zerah: Jeuel and their brethren—six hundred and ninety.” Nehemiah did not repeat this because it had already been recorded in Chronicles. There, however, Ezra gave only the combined total of the descendants of Perez and Zerah: 690. Nehemiah clarified that the descendants of Perez alone numbered 468. From this, together with the account in Chronicles, we learn that the descendants of Zerah alone numbered 222, making a combined total of 690, exactly as stated in Chronicles.

And these were the descendants of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam: In Chronicles it says, “Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah.” Nehemiah found additional distinguished men in Sallu’s genealogy and added that he was the son of Meshullam, son of Joed, and so forth. All these ancestors, extending through Jeshaiah, lived between Meshullam and Hodaviah in the genealogical chain and had been omitted by Ezra. Chronicles also mentions Ibneiah son of Jeroham, Elah son of Uzzi son of Michri, and Meshullam son of Shephatiah, and so forth. Nehemiah omitted all these because he had nothing new to add concerning them, and anyone who read Chronicles already knew of them. He added only to the account in Chronicles the words “and after him, Gabbai and Sallai,” who are not mentioned in Chronicles. There it says, “And their brethren according to their genealogies numbered nine hundred and fifty-six.” Nehemiah teaches us something new: the families of Sallu, Gabbai, and Sallai numbered 928. We can therefore determine that the three additional families mentioned in Chronicles—Ibneiah, Elah, and Meshullam—numbered only twenty-eight people. Together with the 928 members of Sallu’s family, this yields the total recorded in Chronicles.
And Joel, and so forth: This is not mentioned in Chronicles. Nehemiah added information not contained in the earlier book.

Of the priests: In Chronicles (verse 10), it says, “Jedaiah and Jehoiarib.” Nehemiah teaches us that Jedaiah was the son of Jehoiarib, although he and his father were counted as two separate individuals.

Seraiah son of Hilkiah: In Chronicles (verse 11), he is called “Azariah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam.” Hilkiah was the father of Seraiah the High Priest, who was executed by Nebuchadnezzar. Seraiah was the father of Jehozadak, the grandfather of Joshua, who served as High Priest in Nehemiah’s time. Azariah was a grandson of Hilkiah through another son, not through Seraiah the High Priest. His principal name was Seraiah, but in Babylonia he was called Azariah, and Ezra therefore recorded that name in Chronicles. Nehemiah corrected and clarified that his original name was Seraiah. The title “ruler of the House of God” does not mean that he was the High Priest, for Joshua son of Jehozadak was the High Priest, as is well known.

And their brethren: Chronicles further lists Adaiah son of Jeroham, and so forth, and Maasai son of Adiel, and so forth, followed by “and their brethren, heads of their ancestral houses—one thousand seven hundred and sixty.” Nehemiah supplements Ezra’s account by specifying the number belonging to each group. He informs us that Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, and their brethren, who performed the work of the House—that is, the Temple service and its sacrifices—numbered 822. Second, Adaiah son of Jeroham and his brethren numbered 242. [Nehemiah also added three ancestors to Adaiah son of Jeroham’s genealogy whom Ezra had omitted.] There was also Amashsai son of Azarel son of Ahzai, who is not mentioned in Ezra’s account; Nehemiah completed and clarified the record by stating that his group numbered 128. These groups totaled 1,192. We can therefore determine that Maasai son of Adiel and his brethren, the heads of the ancestral houses, numbered 568. This brings the combined total to 1,760, exactly as stated in Chronicles.

And of the Levites: Chronicles lists Shemaiah son of Hasshub, Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, Mattaniah son of Mica son of Zichri son of Asaph, Obadiah son of Shemaiah son of Galal son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah son of Asa son of Elkanah, who lived in the settlements of the Netophathites. It explains neither their respective duties nor their numbers. Nehemiah therefore clarified that Shemaiah son of Hasshub supervised the external work of the House, such as repairs to the Temple structure and the wood for the altar that was brought from outside, as Rashi explains. He also informs us that Shabbethai and Jozabad, whom Ezra did not mention in Chronicles, served together with him. Nehemiah further extended Shemaiah’s genealogy by adding “son of Bunni.” Shemaiah was descended from Merari, as stated in Chronicles. Ezra had mentioned Hashabiah, the head of the genealogical line recorded there (I Chronicles 6:30), while Nehemiah identified the more prominent ancestor Bunni, mentioned there in verse 31, who lived four generations before Hashabiah.

Also: Ezra listed Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, and Mattaniah in that order, implying that Bakbakkar held a higher rank than Mattaniah. Nehemiah therefore informs us that Mattaniah actually ranked first. This is the meaning of “Mattaniah, the chief, who began”: he was first and held the leading position before Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal. His function was “thanksgiving and prayer,” meaning that he led the people in giving thanks and praying. Bakbakkiah was second among his brethren, ranking immediately after Mattaniah and above the other brethren listed in Chronicles—Heresh and Galal—who ranked after Bakbakkiah. Alternatively, “Judah for prayer” may be a personal name: he may have been called “Judah-for-Prayer,” or these may be two separate names, Judah and Letephillah. We similarly find in I Chronicles 25 that Giddalti, Romamti-ezer, and Joshbekashah are all names of individuals. According to this interpretation, he is the same person described below (12:8) as being “over the thanksgiving songs.” The meaning would then be: Mattaniah was the first and chief; Judah-for-Prayer and Bakbakkiah ranked second among their brethren—that is, immediately after Mattaniah. Nehemiah then provides their number, which Chronicles does not record. Together with Abda son of Shammua—the Obadiah son of Shemaiah son of Galal son of Jeduthun mentioned in Chronicles—the Levites numbered 284. The phrase “all the Levites in the holy city” excludes from this count Berechiah son of Asa, whom Chronicles says lived in the settlements of the Netophathites, outside Jerusalem.

And the gatekeepers: Chronicles (verse 17) lists the gatekeepers Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, and Ahiman but does not state their number. Nehemiah therefore explains that the gatekeepers Akkub and Talmon, together with their brethren—namely, Shallum and Ahiman—numbered 172. This number was necessary because, when divided among the seven days of the week, it provided twenty-four Levites for each day, corresponding to the twenty-four watches that guarded the Temple, in addition to the four leaders—Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, and Ahiman—listed in Chronicles.

And the overseer of the Levites: This too is not mentioned in Chronicles, just as it does not mention the overseer of Judah and Benjamin (verse 9) or the overseer of the priests (verse 12). Of the descendants of Asaph, the singers, over the work: He was descended from Asaph, whose family had possessed the privilege, from the days of King David, of serving as overseers of the work of the House of God. The word neged is related to nagid, “leader,” and is an abstract noun denoting leadership or supervision.

For the king’s commandment concerning them: King David had commanded that they should always serve as leaders and overseers, for this entire arrangement had been established from David’s time, as stated there in Chronicles. And there was an appointed master over the singers: He was also an expert in the art of song who taught and supervised the singers day by day, determining which song they should sing and which melody they should perform each day. He was a master of the musical art; the word amanah is related to the expression “the work of a skilled craftsman,” meaning someone proficient in his craft. Alternatively, “the king’s commandment concerning them” means that because they had possessed this privilege since the days of David, the Persian king likewise confirmed their right and commanded that they remain responsible for the service of the House of God.
And Pethahiah: He was appointed by the king over all matters concerning the needs of the people—affairs outside the service of the House of God.

And as for the villages: After identifying those who lived in Jerusalem, the text returns to its earlier statement that in the cities of Judah, each person lived on his ancestral property. The descendants of Judah lived in the cities of Judah, while the descendants of Benjamin lived in the cities of Benjamin.

And divisions of the Levites: That is, they were divided between Judah and Benjamin; the preposition lamed applies to the preceding phrase as well. Some settled among the descendants of Judah and others among the descendants of Benjamin. The Levites had received their cities from the other tribes, since the cities within the territories of Judah and Benjamin had been assigned to the priests (Joshua 21:4). Because the Levites could not settle in their own allotted cities, which were far from Jerusalem, they settled among Judah and Benjamin, as stated below (12:29), that the Levites built villages for themselves around Jerusalem.

And these: The text lists the leaders who served at the time of Zerubbabel’s first return. You will see that everyone mentioned here also signed the covenant above in chapter 10, except that six additional names appear here after Shemaiah. Conversely, six names appear there that are absent here: Zedekiah, Pashhur, Malchijah, Daniel, Baruch, and Meshullam. These six arrived later and, because of their prominence, became heads of the priestly families, displacing the final six listed here. The number is twenty-two in both places, although there should have been twenty-four priestly watches. We must therefore say either that two of those listed also had sons who headed separate watches, or that two sons of Jeshua the High Priest—whom I did not include in the count—served as heads of watches.

And the Levites: Of the Levites who signed the covenant above in chapter 10, only the first four are listed here, while only seventeen Levites signed there. It may be that together with the seven listed in chapter 11, verses 15–20, they comprised the twenty-four heads of the Levitical watches. Alternatively, the five added here beginning with Judah complete a total of twenty-two, corresponding to the number of priestly leaders. The phrase “their brethren opposite them” then refers to Bakbakkiah’s two brethren, Heresh and Galal, who are counted in Chronicles, bringing the total to twenty-four. Al-Hayyadot: In my opinion, this is a proper name; one individual was named Al-Hayyadot. This also appears from the fact that the name Mattaniah is followed by an etnaḥta, separating it from the following words.

And Jeshua fathered Joiakim: All the commentators have found this verse extremely difficult. The Sages stated (Seder Olam, chapter 30; Avodah Zarah 9a) that Persian rule during the Second Temple period lasted thirty-four years—that is, thirty-four years elapsed from the Temple’s construction until the days of Alexander the Great. They also said that Simon the Righteous went out to meet Alexander when he returned from his war with Darius. Simon the Righteous would therefore have belonged to only the second generation after Ezra and Nehemiah, as Maimonides states in his introduction to the Order of Zeraim and as many great authorities have written. How, then, could six generations have been born within such a brief period, especially according to Rashi, who writes that all those listed here served as High Priests? Although the genealogical work says that its authors possessed a tradition that Jaddua was the father of Simon the Righteous, and we do not know the source of that tradition, I nevertheless do not understand the commotion over this difficulty. Who says that all these generations were born during those thirty-four years? Suppose Jeshua son of Jehozadak, who returned from the Babylonian exile and built the Temple, was then 105 years old, and that he and his descendants each fathered a son at the age of fifteen. Simon the Righteous would already have been born when Jeshua was ninety; consequently, when Jeshua built the Temple at the age of 105, Simon would have been fifteen, and by Alexander’s time he would have been forty-five. Even if Jeshua was only ninety when the Temple was built, Simon the Righteous would have been thirty by Alexander’s reign. What, then, is the great difficulty? It is clear from chapter 3 above that when the wall was completed, Eliashib was already called the High Priest. After the Temple was built, Jeshua died and Joiakim was appointed in his place; Joiakim, who was likewise already old, then died and Eliashib was appointed. It is possible that Eliashib and his descendants lived for many years and that, after his death, Simon the Righteous was chosen because he was more worthy than his forefathers. Alternatively, one or two of the intervening descendants may have served as High Priest during that period, or they may all have served only temporarily when the High Priest became ritually impure or under similar circumstances. We therefore need not resort to the strained claim that a later scribe added these words to Nehemiah. Nehemiah, who lived in the days of Jeshua and Joiakim, could already have seen all the later generations, since they had already been born in his lifetime. The same answer can be given concerning the nine generations of Jeconiah’s descendants listed in Chronicles, as will be explained in its proper place.

And in the days of Joiakim: Other heads of the ancestral houses were appointed. Hattush is not included in the list, nor is anyone identified as having replaced Miniamin. It may be that both were still alive and continued serving as heads of their ancestral houses in Joiakim’s time. There is, however, an apparent difficulty. From the statement in chapter 3, “Eliashib the High Priest arose … and they built the Sheep Gate,” it appears that Eliashib was already High Priest when the wall was being rebuilt. How, then, when they made the covenant to observe the Torah in chapter 10, which occurred afterward, could all the former heads of the ancestral houses still have signed it? I offer one of two answers. Either, as explained above, this entire event occurred earlier, at the beginning of their first return in the days of Cyrus; or those men ceased serving as heads of their ancestral houses not because they had died, but because of their advanced age. Nevertheless, they remained more senior and honored than their successors and therefore participated as signatories.

The Levites in the days of Eliashib: This means that in Joiakim’s days, the heads of the priestly ancestral houses changed, but those of the Levites did not. Most of the Levites had not returned in Zerubbabel’s time but had arrived only recently, in Ezra’s time, and therefore still remained at their posts. Only in Eliashib’s days did the heads of the Levitical ancestral houses change. The priests who were subsequently replaced in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan—who is Jonathan—and Jaddua are recorded as heads of ancestral houses elsewhere. Likewise, the priests who were replaced throughout the reign of Darius the Persian are recorded—that is, all the leaders who changed during Darius’s reign. Darius’s period extended from Eliashib’s time until Jaddua’s, for by the beginning of Greek rule Simon the Righteous was already serving, as explained above. The text will now explain where these names were recorded.

The descendants of Levi: This refers to both the priests and the Levites, all of whom were descendants of Levi. Their heads of ancestral houses were recorded in the Book of Chronicles. They possessed a chronicle in which they recorded everything that occurred during that period, including the heads of the ancestral houses of Levi, through the days of Johanan son of Eliashib. This was Jonathan, Eliashib’s grandson. The verse does not say “through the days of Jaddua,” because Jaddua and Johanan served as High Priests during the same period, as explained above.

And the heads of the Levites: This phrase continues into the following verse, which says, “These served in the days of Joiakim.” In the days of Joiakim, Nehemiah, and Ezra—all of whom lived during the same period—the heads of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua. These were among those who had returned with Zerubbabel, as listed in verses 8–9: Sherebiah, Jeshua, Mattaniah, and Bakbakkiah. They are likewise listed in chapters 10 and 11. This accords with what was stated in verse 22, that the Levitical leadership did not change in Joiakim’s time. Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and the others were appointed to offer praise and thanksgiving and supervised the singers and choir leaders. Mattaniah, Bakbakkiah, Obadiah, and the others were gatekeepers who kept watch at the thresholds of the gates—that is, they guarded the entrances, as stated in 11:17–19.
These: These officials were not replaced but continued serving in the days of Joiakim and Nehemiah, for Nehemiah and Ezra lived throughout Joiakim’s lifetime. They died during the days of Eliashib.

And at the dedication they sought out the Levites: That is, the Levites who lived outside Jerusalem. And with thanksgiving processions: These were the two thanksgiving processions through which they consecrated the city, according to the tradition of the Sages.

Upon the wall: This may mean that they walked literally on top of the wall, or it may mean beside the wall, just as “and beside him was the tribe of Manasseh.” The Ritva discusses this question in his commentary on the first chapter of Shevuot and seeks to prove that they walked on top of the wall in order to consecrate its windows and its thickness, according to the opinion that the thickness of the wall is considered part of the city’s interior. And I stationed two great thanksgiving offerings: The Sages received a tradition that these were actual thanksgiving offerings and that consecrating the city required circling it with the loaves of a thanksgiving offering. “Great” refers to the large loaves—the leavened loaves, each of which was made from one-tenth of an ephah, whereas each unleavened loaf was made from one-third of a tenth of an ephah. They also received a tradition that the two thanksgiving offerings proceeded either side by side or one behind the other, and that one was eaten while the other was burned. At first sight, however, the plain meaning of the verse appears to contradict this tradition, for Scripture indicates that half the people proceeded from left to right while the other half proceeded from right to left. I have already explained this thoroughly above in chapter 3. Nehemiah’s residence was at the Valley Gate, in the center of the western wall, and the processions began there. The half that turned to the right proceeded toward the Dung Gate, continued to the stairs of the City of David and the southwestern extremity, and from there followed the entire southern wall from west to east until reaching the Water Gate at the southeastern side, as described in verses 31–37 and above in 3:13–26. Those who proceeded from right to left went from the Valley Gate to the Tower of the Ovens on the northwestern side, as stated above in 3:12. From there, they traveled west to east along the northern wall, passing the Broad Wall and the Ephraim Gate until they reached the Old Gate at the northeastern corner, as described there in verses 6–8. They then proceeded southward along the eastern side and stopped at the Sheep Gate, in the center of the eastern wall, as described there in verses 1–6. Those who had turned to the right approached them from the south, and the two groups met on the eastern side at the Guard Gate. This is required by the plain meaning of the verses and cannot be interpreted otherwise; the Sages likewise understood the verses in this manner. The truth is that they divided the loaves of the two thanksgiving offerings, each of which contained ten loaves. They took five loaves from each offering and carried them in the procession that circled to the right, along the southern side; they likewise took five loaves from each offering and carried them in the procession circling along the northern side. Thus, both sides were encircled with loaves from both thanksgiving offerings. This is required by the statement, “Hoshaiah went behind them.” If only one thanksgiving offering had proceeded in each direction, the verse should have said, “He went behind it.” The plural confirms the Sages’ teaching that both thanksgiving offerings proceeded on the right-hand route as well. We can therefore explain the verses as follows: Nehemiah says that he brought up the officials of Judah—all the officials together—and stationed them with the two thanksgiving offerings. At the place where they ascended by the Valley Gate stood the two great thanksgiving offerings, meaning the ten leavened loaves from each offering. They were then divided into two processions: five loaves from each offering proceeded to the right, from north to south. Hoshaiah went behind them—behind the portions of both thanksgiving offerings that proceeded to the right—together with half the officials of Judah. At that point, the officials divided, half proceeding to the right. Azariah, Ezra, and the others went with them, together with some of the priestly families, while Ezra the Scribe went before them—that is, before the priests. They continued in this manner until reaching the Water Gate on the eastern side, near the Guard Gate.

And the thanksgiving offering: This still refers to the procession that went toward the right. According to the opinion that the two thanksgiving offerings proceeded side by side, the verse calls it “the second thanksgiving offering that proceeded opposite” the first—that is, beside it—and Nehemiah walked alone behind this offering. According to the opinion that the offerings proceeded one behind the other, the word “opposite” refers to the offering that followed behind the first. As stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 1:3), one Sage understood “he sits opposite him” to mean beside him, while the other inferred from “he shall pinch off its head opposite its nape” that “opposite” can mean behind. According to this interpretation, Nehemiah walked immediately behind the final thanksgiving offering, with the officials following him; Ezra then followed, with the priests behind him. The text now describes the portions of the two thanksgiving offerings that proceeded toward the left. Thus it says, “and half the people walked upon the wall, above the Tower of the Ovens,” and they stopped at the Guard Gate.

And they stood: Nehemiah and the half of the officials accompanying him, who had approached from the south and stopped at the Water Gate, then drew near to the thanksgiving processions that had arrived from the north. And the two thanksgiving processions stood in the House of God, for there the two groups met one another. And I and half the officials were there, for Nehemiah had approached from the south. And the priests—Eliakim, Maaseiah, and the others—came with trumpets from the north to meet them, as did Maaseiah and Shemaiah. The singers then raised their voices, and Jezrahiah was the overseer responsible for the songs and melodies performed on that occasion.

Great sacrifices: This may mean numerous sacrifices, or fattened and exceptionally large bulls. For God had caused them to rejoice: Their joy did not result merely from the festive meals they held; it was a God-given joy so profound that even the children rejoiced.

And they appointed: They appointed officials over the chambers in which the terumah, the first portion—meaning the first fruits—and the tithes were stored. Previously, the Levites had traveled through the cities to collect the tithes, as explained above (10:38–39). Now, however, the portions—that is, the gifts prescribed by the Torah for the priests and also for the Levites—would be brought into the storehouses. For Judah rejoiced greatly over the priests and Levites who stood at their service. They kept the charge of their God and the charge of purification, as the Torah says, “They shall keep your charge and the charge of the Tent.” These included the singers and the gatekeepers. Although their particular organization was not prescribed by the Torah, David and Solomon had established it. The people therefore recognized that the Levites actively performing the Temple service should take precedence over the other Levites. Consequently, they appointed officials so that the tithe too would be brought into the chambers and distributed among the Levites serving in the House of God.

For in the days of David: At that time, it was established who would serve as singers. Asaph and his descendants had held this role from early times and consistently served as the leaders of the singers. The songs and melodies were also instituted then, including songs of praise and songs of thanksgiving.

And all Israel: Until then, although they provided portions for the gatekeepers, they gave the tithes directly to the Levites. Each Levite collected his tithe in the fields and then separated the tithe of the tithe for the descendants of Aaron. They now enacted that the tithes should no longer be given to Levites who went around collecting them at the threshing floors; instead, they were to be brought to the appointed officials, who would distribute them among the Levites serving in the House of God.

On that day: This occurred on the day mentioned below, when Nehemiah threw out Tobiah’s belongings. Tobiah was also an Ammonite and was related by marriage to the leaders of the people, who had intermarried with him, as stated above (6:18). Nehemiah then commanded that they read from the Book of Moses—that is, Deuteronomy, which Moses delivered and which contains this prohibition.

For they did not meet them: If they were genuinely afraid of you—which might have provided some excuse for their subsequently hiring Balaam—they should instead have met you with bread and water and sought peace and a covenant with you. If they withheld bread because they were not afraid of you, then why did they hire Balaam? Nor can one argue that Balaam’s curse was ineffective and therefore caused no harm, for the verse says, “Our God transformed the curse into a blessing.” Had God not done so, Balaam’s curse would have caused harm.

And it came to pass: They then separated from Israel the entire mixed multitude—that is, the Ammonite and Moabite converts who had mingled among them. Although we maintain that the nations have now become intermixed and that anyone who separates from a group is presumed to come from its majority, as Rabbi Joshua states in tractate Yadayim and as cited in Berakhot 28a, it may be that at that time certain Ammonites were still identifiable by their lineage. The principal intermingling of the nations was caused by Nebuchadnezzar, as Tosafot explain in Megillah 12b and Yevamot 76b. Although this occurred after the destruction, some members of these nations still remained unmixed and identifiable.

And before this: The text explains what prompted them to read from Deuteronomy on that particular day. Eliashib the priest had his chamber near Tobiah’s chamber, for he had prepared a large chamber for Tobiah beside his own. Previously, that chamber had been used to store the grain offering and the other sacred provisions. At that time, however, the people had ceased giving the terumot and tithes, leaving the chamber empty, so the priest allowed Tobiah to live there.

And during all this: This occurred while I was absent from Jerusalem, when these breaches in observance arose. And after some time: The king had summoned Nehemiah and commanded him to remain at his side for a fixed period. When that period ended, I requested leave from the king—that is, I obtained his permission to return. And I came to Jerusalem and perceived the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah: He had acted for Tobiah’s benefit by desecrating the Temple.

And it displeased me greatly, and I threw out: Because Tobiah’s relatives and the officials protested against Nehemiah’s action, he ordered the Torah to be read aloud to show them that Tobiah was forbidden to enter the congregation.

And I said, and I restored the vessels of the House of God there: This chamber had originally contained the vessels, the grain offering, and the frankincense, as explained above in verse 5, and Nehemiah returned these items to their proper place. He also wished to restore there the tithes and terumah that had previously been stored there. From this, he discovered that the people were no longer giving their tithes and terumot, as the following verse explains.

And I learned that the portions of the Levites—that is, their allotted shares—had not been given. The singular form refers to the act of giving. And they fled: Consequently, the Levites abandoned their assigned duties and went away to work in their fields.
And I gathered them: I assembled the Levites and restored them to their assigned duties. All Israel then began giving the tithes as they had previously.

And I appointed as treasurers: The verb is transitive even though it appears in the simple qal conjugation. Many verbs that ordinarily occur only in the qal may sometimes be intransitive and sometimes transitive. This differs from Radak’s interpretation.

Remember me: Nehemiah now relates that the people violated all three obligations they had accepted upon themselves under oath above in chapter 10: bringing the tithes, observing the Sabbath, and separating from foreign women. They transgressed all three while Nehemiah was absent from Jerusalem, and he restored each one to its proper observance. The first time, they had accepted these obligations through Ezra or on their own initiative, so the merit had not been attributed to Nehemiah. Now, however, after observance had broken down, Nehemiah erected a protective fence, stood in the breach, and restored everything to its proper state. He therefore asked that this merit be credited to him as an act of righteousness, as though he had established the entire observance from the beginning. Thus he says, “for this”—because I repaired the breach, remember the entire accomplishment as though I alone had brought it about.

In those days: This observance likewise broke down while Nehemiah was away from Jerusalem. Treading: The verse lists the transgressions from the most severe to the less severe. Treading winepresses on the Sabbath is an offense punishable by stoning. Bringing heaps of produce and loading them: It may be that they loaded the produce on Friday and transported it on the Sabbath, thereby violating the obligation that one’s animals rest. And I warned them on the day when they sold provisions: They had designated the Sabbath as market day. Nehemiah therefore warned them on the day regularly appointed for selling food and provisions that they must not sell on that day.

And the Tyrians: Consequently, foreign merchants came, settled there, and sold their goods on the Sabbath, because they paid no heed to the prohibition against buying and selling, which is not explicitly stated in the Torah.
And I contended: He therefore rebuked the officials for failing to protest against this conduct, since responsibility for the transgression rested upon them.

When the shadows fell: That is, when the shadows lengthened on Friday afternoon, after midday. No one should enter: The phrase “and I said” applies to this clause as well. Nehemiah said that no burden should enter—the gate was not to be opened for anyone carrying a burden.
And they lodged outside: They remained there so that the city’s inhabitants could come out, purchase small items from them, and smuggle them into the city.

And I said: He commanded that the Levites guard the gates on the Sabbath. He explained that this formed part of the Sabbath’s sanctity: its guards should be Levites, who were purer, more careful to avoid wrongdoing, and more vigilant in preserving the Sabbath’s holiness.
Also: The text now relates that they violated the third obligation they had accepted under oath by marrying foreign women.

And half of their children: The meaning is that they spoke half in the language of Ashdod. Their speech was a mixture—half Judean and half Ashdodite. Consequently, they did not know any language properly: they could neither speak Judean nor speak the language of any particular people, because their speech combined two languages, the language of their father and that of their mother.
And I contended with them: Afterward, I cursed them, and then I struck some of them. He progressively increased the severity of the punishments.

Was it not: Because the Torah explains the prohibition by saying, “For he will turn your son away from following Me,” they claimed that they could be trusted not to abandon the Torah because of their foreign wives. Nehemiah replied: Did Solomon not likewise say, “I will sin, but I will not turn away”? It should have been easier for him than for anyone else to remain faithful—both because of his greatness, for there was no king like him, and because of his righteousness, for he was beloved by his God. Nevertheless, he did not maintain his righteousness, and the foreign women caused even him to sin. Shall we then listen to you and accept your claim that your hearts will not turn away, thereby allowing you to commit all this great evil and act unfaithfully toward our God by marrying foreign women?

And I drove him away: Nehemiah could not strike him because he was a powerful and violent man. He therefore said: Since I could not compel him by force, may God punish him for defiling the priesthood. Through his actions, he became polluted and excluded both from the priesthood, so that he could no longer serve in the Temple, and from the covenant of the priesthood, for he forfeited his priestly lineage and his children became non-priests.
And I purified them: After purifying them from every foreign influence, I established the priestly and Levitical watches.

And for the wood offering: After restoring everything they had undertaken by oath above in chapter 10, Nehemiah also restored these practices, for there they had sworn concerning the wood offering (verse 35) and the first fruits (verse 37). Therefore, he said, “Remember me, my God, for good,” as explained above in verse 14.
